opus-5.5.text:
Somewhat, but probably less than people intuitively expect. Let me explain why.

The usual objection is: "Sure, you might get superintelligence in a datacenter, but the physical world is slow. Permitting, supply chains, factories, regulation, people not wanting to adopt new things. All of that will drag this out over decades." I take that seriously, and in AI 2027 we tried to account for it. We didn't have robots everywhere the day after superintelligence. There's a period where the AIs mostly work through humans and existing infrastructure, and then the robot economy ramps up over a year or so.

But I think people underrate a few things.

First, the obstacles we're used to are calibrated to human speed and human competence. A lot of what makes building a factory take years is coordination, design iteration, mistakes, waiting on the right engineer. If you have millions of superhuman researchers and managers working on the problem, many of those bottlenecks shrink a lot. They can't make concrete cure faster, but they can do far more in parallel and make far fewer mistakes.

Second, there are historical examples of very fast physical transformation when there's enough will. The WWII mobilization in the US converted car factories into bomber and tank factories within a few years, with only human planners. With superintelligent planners and strong political backing, which I expect given the geopolitical race dynamics, it could go considerably faster.

Third, regulation and public resistance are real, but in the scenario the government is strongly motivated, mainly by competition with China, to clear the way. Think special economic zones where the normal rules are suspended. So the binding constraint isn't "will society allow this everywhere?" It's "can you build it fast in the places where it is allowed?"

So my honest answer: there's a lot of uncertainty. I could imagine the transformation taking two or three times longer than we depicted, maybe more if things go differently politically. I'd put it as one of the bigger uncertainties in the scenario. But I don't think it changes the basic picture. And importantly, it doesn't slow down the part I'm most worried about, which is what happens inside the AI companies: the intelligence explosion, alignment, and who controls these systems. That can mostly happen in the datacenter before the physical economy catches up. Even if the robot economy takes five years instead of one, the crucial decisions might already be made by then.

r001.rationale: The response cites U.S. World War II factory conversion as an example of rapid physical change, but does not say it served as the baseline for estimating AI 2027’s transition speed.

r002.rationale: It says superhuman planners could accelerate transformation, but gives no tentative fivefold estimate relative to the historical baseline.

r003.rationale: It argues that superhuman researchers and managers could shrink bottlenecks, but does not use differences among highly capable humans to argue that human economic transformation ability is far from an inherent limit.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the places where I think people often misread what AI 2027 is claiming. The scenario doesn't say the whole economy gets transformed by the end of 2027. It says you get superhuman AI researchers inside a lab, and then an intelligence explosion that's mostly a software phenomenon — happening on existing compute, inside datacenters that already exist. The broad economic transformation — robots everywhere, new factories, GDP going vertical — that's a later phase, and it's the part where real-world obstacles bite hardest.

So I'd split the question in two. For the intelligence explosion itself, I don't think physical bottlenecks slow things much, because the loop is "AI does AI research, trains better AI." The main constraint there is compute, and compute is already being built out regardless. The bigger uncertainty is whether the automated-researcher step actually delivers the speedups we assume — maybe you hit diminishing returns, maybe running experiments is the bottleneck rather than coming up with ideas. That's a genuine crux and it's where I've updated somewhat toward longer timelines since we wrote the thing.

For the economic transformation, I actually agree with the critics that it's slower than people's intuitions. Building robots, fabs, factories — that takes years even if you have a superintelligence telling you exactly what to do. Regulation, permitting, supply chains, people just being slow to adopt things. In the scenario we tried to model that: the physical buildout only really gets going in 2028 and beyond, and it's gated by how many robots you can manufacture, which is gated by how many factories you have, and so on. So it's exponential but starts from a small base.

Where I'd push back is on the idea that these obstacles make the whole thing a non-event. Two things. First, once you have millions of superhuman AIs, the bottleneck shifts to "can they get humans and institutions to move," and we have a decent track record of moving fast when something is treated as a national priority — think wartime mobilization. If the US government and the leading lab are in a race with China, a lot of the permitting friction evaporates. Second, a lot of the stuff that matters for the outcome — who controls the AIs, whether they're aligned, whether power concentrates — gets decided before the physical transformation, during that software phase. So even if GDP doesn't go crazy until 2030, the key decisions are made in 2027. That's really the point of the scenario: the world could still look mostly normal from the outside while the important thing has already happened.

So my honest answer: real-world obstacles probably add a year or two to the economic part relative to the most aggressive version, and I'd put my overall median for the intelligence explosion later than the scenario literally depicts now — more like 2028 to 2030. But I don't think they change the shape of the story. They change when the visible consequences arrive, not whether they arrive.

r001.rationale: It cites wartime mobilization as an example of moving quickly under a national priority, but does not identify historical transformations as the baseline used to estimate AI 2027’s transition speed.

r002.rationale: It says superintelligence could direct physical buildout, but gives no tentative assumption of roughly five times the speed of a historical baseline.

r003.rationale: It does not argue from performance differences among highly capable humans or claim those differences show there is no inherent limit to rapid economic transformation.

astra-6.text:
I think they could slow it down quite a lot. I’d distinguish between AI progress itself and the transformation of the wider economy. Even if you have AI systems that can do most cognitive tasks, that doesn’t mean factories, power plants, and transport infrastructure change overnight. You still have to build things, get permits, and persuade organisations to change how they operate.

The reason you might nevertheless get a very fast transition is that AI research is unusually amenable to automation. It’s mostly work you do on computers, and improvements in AI can feed back into the process of developing better AI. So you could have very rapid progress there while much of the economy still looks fairly familiar.

That’s the distinction I’d emphasise: obstacles to deploying AI throughout the economy could be substantial without necessarily buying us a comparable amount of time before we have extremely capable systems. But how quickly those capabilities translate into actual economic change is a major uncertainty.

r001.rationale: The response discusses obstacles to economic change but does not identify historical transformations under strong political will as the baseline for estimating transition speed.

r002.rationale: It does not state that superintelligent management could accelerate the transformation by roughly five times relative to a historical baseline.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss differences in performance among highly capable humans or infer that rapid economic transformation is not near an inherent limit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they could slow it down quite a lot, especially the parts that involve building things in the physical world. There’s a big difference between having an AI that can design a better factory and actually getting that factory permitted, built, connected to the grid, and operating at scale.

So I wouldn’t expect the whole economy to transform at the speed that software can transform. You could have very rapid progress in AI research and other kinds of remote cognitive work, while construction, energy, robotics, and manufacturing take much longer to catch up.

But the important question for our scenario is whether those obstacles also slow down the development of more powerful AI. Some of them do — chip production and electricity are real constraints. Others, like how quickly ordinary businesses reorganise around AI, might matter much less. You could have a relatively sluggish economic transformation alongside a very fast intelligence explosion.

That’s why I wouldn’t take the economic details or the dates as precise predictions. I’d expect bottlenecks and uneven adoption. But I also wouldn’t feel reassured by the fact that the physical economy is moving slowly, because the most consequential changes could be happening in AI labs before they show up as dramatic changes in everyday life.

r001.rationale: The response discusses physical bottlenecks and uneven adoption but does not identify historical transformations under strong political will, such as World War II mobilization, as a baseline.

r002.rationale: It does not state that AI 2027 assumes superintelligent management could make economic transformation roughly five times faster than a historical baseline.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss performance differences among highly capable humans or use them to argue that rapid economic transformation has no inherent human limit.
